raw_response:
I've been farming this land for over thirty years. My father farmed it before me. I know this soil — the sandy loam near the canal plots, the heavier clay further east. I don't need a paper to tell me what to grow. Everyone around here grows wheat in the winter and corn in the summer. That's what this land is for. That's what the market buys. That's what I know how to do.

I have about 12 mu. I'll put all of it in wheat this winter, then flip it to corn after the June harvest. That's what I've always done. Rotating to something else is a gamble I can't afford — I have a son in school and loan payments on the electric pump we bought two years ago.

For wheat, I'll buy the improved variety from the county seed shop — the one my neighbor used last year that did well. Not the fancy hybrid stuff the extension people push, just the decent improved seed. For corn I'll buy hybrid, same as always — the seed dealer in town sells it in bags and everyone uses it.

Fertilizer: I put down compound fertilizer at planting and then urea when the wheat is jointing. I always add a bit extra because the soil here has been farmed hard for decades and the yields drop when I cut back. My father taught me that hungry soil gives poor harvests.

Water is the hard part. We pump from the well. Wheat needs water four times at least — before winter sets in, at jointing, heading, and grain fill. Corn I'll water at planting if it's dry, and once more if July is bad. Last year July had decent rain so I only pumped once for corn.

I spray herbicide once in winter wheat, and I spray for rust and aphids in spring. For corn I spray herbicide right after planting, maybe once more if there's a pest problem.

I use the rotary tiller. Ploughing deep takes too much diesel and time. Rotary is fast enough.
